content: The process for achieving the expected throughput in HIV testing involves several key steps: 1. Preand Post-Test Information: This includes providing clients with information before and after testing, as well as linking them to appropriate services. Further details can be found in Chapter 4 of the referenced guidelines. 2. Pre-Analytical Phase: This step involves collecting and processing specimens and recording client details accurately. 3. Analytical Phase: This includes performing the assay procedure and documenting the results. 4. Post-Analytical Phase: This involves interpreting the test results and reporting the client’s HIV status. Throughput refers to the number of tests conducted daily, which depends on the number of individuals tested and the expected positivity rate. Roles and Responsibilities at Testing Sites The roles of all personnel at the testing site must be clearly defined. This includes specifying who collects specimens, performs tests, conducts quality control (QC), issues reports, double-checks results, manages data entry, and handles cleaning. National regulations often determine which health worker cadres can perform specific functions. All personnel should receive both pre-service and in-service training, with ongoing education to maintain and improve skills, especially at sites with low client throughput or infrequent testing schedules. Regular supportive supervision and mentoring are essential, as is ensuring the psychological and physical well-being of HIV testing providers. Good vision is critical for reading subjective assays like rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Implementation Recommendations Maintain training checklists to document staff proficiency. Conduct annual performance appraisals to address any issues affecting task performance. Equipment Requirements Regardless of the testing location or assay format, fully functional and appropriate equipment is essential. For RDT-based services, good lighting, timing devices, and a paper-lined surface are necessary. If ambient temperatures exceed manufacturer recommendations, monitored refrigerators are required for storage. For laboratory-based in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), equipment calibration and maintenance are critical for accurate results. Implementation Recommendations for Equipment Monitor storage and testing areas with thermometers. Perform preventive and corrective maintenance on equipment as needed. Clearly label and remove non-functional equipment from service. Develop standard operating procedures (SOPs) for equipment use, cleaning, and maintenance. Purchasing and Inventory Management Stock-outs of HIV test kits or essential consumables can lead to poor-quality results, missed opportunities, and client dissatisfaction. A lack of assays compromises diagnostic accuracy. For example, using fewer assays than required may result in inaccurate HIV status determination. A system (logistics management information system or paper-based) is needed at each site to track test kits, reagents, and consumables. Proper storage, noting expiration dates, and reordering in advance are critical to avoid stock-outs. Implementation Recommendations for Inventory Establish a stock recording system and SOPs. Maintain an inventory of required items. Avoid splitting test kits or interchanging components between kits. QC involves detecting, evaluating, and correcting errors before reporting results. It includes pre-analytical checks (e.g., room temperature and stock availability), analytical checks (e.g., running QC specimens), and post-analytical checks (e.g., double-checking HIV status reports and data entry). Implementation Recommendations for QC Establish criteria for specimen acceptance, storage, and referral. Use external third-party QC materials in addition to internal QC. Run external QC specimens weekly, with new operators, new test kit lots, or when environmental conditions deviate from recommendations. Information Management Information management involves recording, storing, and retrieving data, including test results and client reminders. Testing personnel must minimize transcription errors. Discrepancies between readers should be resolved by a third reader. Documentation and Records Documents include policies, procedures, and work instructions for all aspects of testing services. These should be approved, reviewed annually, and updated as needed. Records generated from testing activities must be securely stored for up to five years and readily retrievable for retesting or referrals. Implementation Recommendations for Documentation Develop SOPs for all procedures, including specimen collection, testing algorithms, and QC. Maintain equipment maintenance and temperature records. Keep laboratory logbooks and forms for reporting HIV status. Occurrence Management Occurrence management involves detecting and documenting non-conformances and implementing corrective actions. Non-conformances may include procedural lapses or deviations from documented protocols. Data sources such as internal audits, supervisory reports, and QC data can help identify issues. Implementation Recommendations for Occurrence Management Establish a system to monitor and address quality issues. Create a user feedback form for product issues. Monitor indicators such as turnaround times, invalid result rates, and stock-outs. Internal audits, conducted at least annually, involve observing testing practices and identifying areas for improvement. External quality assessment (EQA) schemes, such as proficiency testing, are essential for ensuring accuracy and reliability. Implementation Recommendations for Assessment Participate in EQA schemes with accredited providers. Follow up on unacceptable EQA results with corrective actions. Process Improvement Testing services should identify areas for improvement, implement changes, and evaluate their impact. Corrective actions address root causes of problems, while preventive actions reduce the likelihood of recurrence. Data from QC and EQA activities can guide these actions. Implementation Recommendations for Process Improvement Site supervisors should proactively identify improvement opportunities and communicate them to higher management levels. Client Service Ensuring client satisfaction involves meeting expectations for quality and delivering accurate results promptly. Services should be inclusive and non-discriminatory, addressing the specific needs of key populations. Privacy and confidentiality are critical. Implementation Recommendations for Client Service Collect client feedback through exit interviews or suggestion boxes. Train staff to provide non-stigmatizing and inclusive services. Facilities and Safety Testing sites should be clean, comfortable, and well-lit, with proper waste disposal systems. Universal precautions must be observed to protect clients and staff from harm. Quality Improvement Quality assurance is an ongoing process. Testing providers and managers must continuously monitor and evaluate their programs to improve services. Stakeholder involvement at all levels is essential for maintaining a functional quality management system (QMS).
